Fabrication of ternary deep eutectic solvent choline chloride:_p_-toluene sulfonic acid:Glycerol for pretreating wheat straw to augment cellulose accessibility, xylan removal, and lignin removal
Zhuo Zhang¹, Qianqian Gao¹, Yu-Cai He*
School of Pharmacy & School of Biological and Food Engineering, Changzhou University, Changzhou, 213164, China
ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Cellulose accessibility Lignin removal Xylan removal

ABSTRACT In this research, a novel ternary deep eutectic solvent (TDES) ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly (1:1:1), composed of choline chloride (ChCl), p-toluene sulfonic acid (p-TsOH), and glycerol (Gly), was successfully fabricated and adopted to pretreat wheat straw under relatively mild conditions (80 °C, 45 min) for removing xylan (99.9 %), eliminating lignin (88.5 %) and elevating subsequent enzymatic saccharification efficiency (98.1 %). The combined hydrolysis factor and combined delignification factor quantitatively predicted the dissolution kinetics of residual xylan and residual lignin, respectively, with high accuracy. Following ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly treatment, the accessibility of cellulose in wheat straw elevated considerably to 691.5 mg dye/g cellulose, while surface lignin area diminished to 134.6 m²/g and lignin hydrophobicity was weakened to 2.6 L/g. These structural and surface property modifications contributed to the enhancement of enzymolysis. Molecular dynamics simulations and quantum chemical calculations were adopted to reveal van der Waals interactions between ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly and lignin, as well as dispersion interactions between ChCl and lignin, consequently elucidating the molecular-level interaction mechanism between lignocellulose and ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly. In summary, this study achieved effectual pretreatment of wheat straw using the TDES ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly but also considerably promoted the depolymerization of lignocellulosic biomass in biorefining processes, offering new insights into the value-added utilization of biomass resources.

1. Introduction To date, the development of clean energy alternatives has emerged as a critical priority [1,2]. Lignocellulosic biomass exhibits considerable potential for manufacturing bio-based materials, bioethanol, and bio-diesel [3,4]. Wheat straw (WS), a widely available byproduct of global wheat cultivation, is often treated as waste, yet it contains a significant amount of polysaccharides, primarily composed of approximately 70 % sugar compounds, including cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin [5,6]. Nevertheless, the complex structural interactions between cellulose and hemicellulose hinder enzymatic digestion [7,8]. Accordingly, it is essential to develop and select appropriate pretreatment strategies to overcome the recalcitrance of lignocellulosic materials and facilitate their effective disintegration [9].
Recently, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged as promising green solvents to pretreat biomass due to their tailorable hydrogen-

For instance, Li et al. reported an acidic binary DES composed of ChCl/ oxalic acid (molar ratio 3:1) that achieved 84% delignification and 96% enzymolysis efficiency after optimized treatment (130 °C, 1 h) of rape- seed straw [13]. Similarly, Tang et al. demonstrated that pretreatment with an acidic binary DES system of cetyltrimethylammonium bromide/ glycerol (molar ratio 1:6, 200 °C, 90 min) resulted in 46 % delignifica- tion and 53% xylan removal from rapeseed straw [14]. Recent studies indicated that incorporating a third component (such as alcoholic compounds, Lewis acids) into binary DESs to form ternary DESs (TDESs) can considerably improve biomass pretreatment efficiency [15–17]. Introducing a third component markedly modulates the physicochem- ical features of the solvent system (such as viscosity and dissolving ca- pacity), consequently improving mass transfer rates and overall pretreatment efficiency [18,19]. Compared to conventional thermochemical methods which typically require reaction temperatures exceeding 200 °C to achieve effective biomass decompo- sition, TDES based approaches enable efficient biomass conversion under significantly milder conditions (e.g., 80–120 °C). This substantial reduction in operating temperature not only directly diminishes energy input requirements but also mitigates additional costs associated with high-temperature-resistant equipment, thereby achieving considerable energy savings. Furthermore, the mild reaction conditions minimize excessive degradation of high-value components within the biomass, enhancing selectivity toward target products. Collectively, these ad- vantages position TDES-mediated processes as a more sustainable technological pathway for biomass valorization. For example, Zhao et al. fabricated a TDES using octadecyl dimethyl ammonium chloride, pro- pionic acid, and p-toluenesulfonic acid (p-TsOH), achieving effectual pretreatment of sorghum straw under relatively mild conditions with an enzymolysis efficiency of 69.3% [23]. Zhang et al. prepared a TDES from choline chloride (ChCl), N-(2-hydroxyethyl)ethylenediamine (NE), and iron(III) chloride for corn stover treatment under mild conditions, achieving 87% delignification [24]. Similarly, He et al. reported that a TDES composed of ChCl, glycerol (Gly), and aluminum chloride removed 70.8% lignin and 87.7% hemicellulose from reed straw [25]. Consequently, TDES technology enables the effectual conversion of previously underutilized biomass resources, apparently broadening the scope of biorefinery feedstocks and opening new pathways toward enhancing the economic viability and sustainability of full biomass component utilization.

This work aimed to develop an effectual pretreatment process for wheat straw (WS) based on a DES system composed of choline chloride (ChCl), p-toluenesulfonic acid (p-TsOH), and glycerol (Gly), with the objective of enhancing its physicochemical properties and microstructural characteristics. The two-phase combined hydrolysis factor (CHF) model and the combined delignification factor (CDF) model can be utilized to quantitatively characterize the processes of hemicellulose dissolution and lignin removal, respectively. The effectiveness of the pretreatment can be estimated by analyzing variations in component content and enzymolysis performance, while key operational parameters—such as performance temperature, operation duration, and molar ratio—are systematically optimized. The response surface methodology can be adopted to determine the optimal DES-treatment conditions and to estimate the enzymatic digestion rate as a response variable. Systematically investigating the regulatory of the pretreatment on influencing cellulose accessibility, surface lignin coverage, and hydrophobicity can be implemented to assess the impacts on the subsequent enzymolysis efficiency. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and other analytical techniques may be utilized to characterize the structural and compositional alterations in WS before and after DES treatment, consequently elucidating the mechanisms underlying lignin removal and enhanced enzymolysis. To explore the interaction mechanisms between biomass and DES at the molecular level, molecular dynamics simulations can be adopted, offering theoretical insights for the development of efficient biomass pretreatment strategies. Overall, this study presents a comprehensive analysis and in-depth discussion of the ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly-based biomass pretreatment process.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Preparation of DESs ChCl, _p_-TsOH, and glycerol were blended at varying molar ratios (1:1:0.5, 1:1:1, 1:1:2, 1:1:3). Concurrently, ChCl and _p_-TsOH were individually combined with ethylene glycol (EG) at a molar ratio of 1:1:1. The DES preparation was implemented at 80 °C for 15 to 30 min,
and the obtained homogeneous and transparent liquids were used to pretreat WS without further purification.

## 2.2. Treatment of WS with DESS In a three-necked flask, 60 g of TDES and 6 g of WS were mixed, resulting in a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:10 (w/w). The mixture was stirred uniformly in an oil bath at a pre-determined temperature range of 40–120 °C for a variable duration of 30–75 min.

## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. The determination of K-T parameters of TDESs The Kamlet-Taft parameters are empirical descriptors adopted to characterize the microscopic properties of solvent molecules and to quantitatively assess the specific interactions between solvents and solutes [26]. In this study, we systematically investigated the effects of EG) and Gly as hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) on the solvation properties of DES-ChCl. Specifically, EG and Gly were introduced into the DES-ChCl system at identical molar ratios, and the Kamlet-Taft parameters of the resulting binary DESs (designated as TDES$_{EG}$ and TDES$_{Gly}$, respectively) were accurately measured (Table 1). The experimental results clearly demonstrated that, compared with TDES$_{EG}$, TDES$_{Gly}$ exhibited significantly higher hydrogen bond donor ability (α value), hydrogen bond acceptor ability (β value), and dipolarity/polarizability (π* value). This notable difference in solvation properties is primarily attributed to the fundamental structural differences between Gly and EG—specifically, Gly contains an additional hydroxyl (-OH) functional group compared to EG. This additional hydroxyl group exerts a dual influence: first, it enhances the acidity of glycerol, providing more hydrogen bond donor sites and thereby directly increasing its hydrogen bond donor ability (α value); second, due to the high electronegativity of the oxygen atom, this hydroxyl group also significantly enhances Gly's capacity as a hydrogen bond acceptor (β value) [27]. Moreover, the molecular structure of glycerol is more complex, and its electron cloud distribution is more responsive to external electric fields, leading to greater polarizability, which is reflected in the significantly elevated π* value [27]. Given the overall advantages of TDES$_{Gly}$ in terms of α, β, and π* parameters—factors directly associated with the dissolution capacity, catalytic activity, and interaction strength with substrates (e.g., biomass) of DESs—Gly was selected as the optimal third component for constructing a novel TDES system in combination with ChCl and p-TsOH, based on its superior solvation characteristics.

The molar ratio of DES is a critical factor influencing the Kamlet-Taft parameters. In this work, TDESGly was prepared with varying molar ratios (1:1:0.5, 1:1:1, 1:1:2, 1:1:3), and the impacts of these ratios on the Kamlet-Taft parameter values were systematically estimated. As the molar ratio of glycerol (Gly) elevated, the α and π* values of the Kamlet-Taft parameters gradually increased, whereas the β value showed a corresponding decrease (Table 1). The hydroxyl groups in glycerol are capable of forming hydrogen-bonds with the sulfonic acid oxygen atoms of p-TsOH or the cationic moiety of ChCl in DES-ChCl, consequently

3.2. Investigating biomass chemical component variations under different ternary DES treatment The primary objective of pretreatment is to overcome the structural and compositional barriers inherent to biomass, consequently aug- menting the accessibility of biomass to reaction reagents by elevating the contact area and availability of reactive sites [29]. In this research, the impacts of two different TDES, namely TDESEG and TDESGly, on WS before and after DES treatment were estimated. Additionally, key pre- treatment parameters—such as the molar ratio of DES components, temperature, and treatment duration—were optimized. As shown in Fig. 1, the glucan content in raw WS was 38.2%. After treatment with TDESEG and TDESGly, the glucan content in the WS solid residue increased to 70.2% and 73.3%, respectively. These results indicate that the incorporation of a third component considerably enhanced the glucan content in WS following DES treatment. Compared to binary DES-ChCl alone, supplementing the third component to form TDES could improve the removal ability of WS xylan, resulting in a reduction in xylan content in the WS solid residue. This improvement may be attributed to the introduction of glycerol, which potentially alters the hydrogen-bond network structure of DES, consequently enhancing its capability to dissolve lignin and hemicellulose in WS [29]. As a result, the WS lignin and xylan were more effectually dissolved and removed, exposing the glucan that was originally embedded within the WS lignocellulosic matrix, leading to an increased glucan content [30].

TDESGly had a remarkable impact on the retention of WS glucan and the removal of lignin and xylan (Fig. 1). Under identical treatment conditions (80 °C, 60 min), compared to treatment with DES (ChCl:p-TsOH, mol:mol 1:1), TDESGly (ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly, mol:mol:mol 1:1:1) formed by supplementing Gly to this DES increased the glucan content in the DES-pretreated WS from 62.6% to 73.3%. The results manifested that supplementing glycerol not only effectually separated xylan and lignin from WS but also greatly retained glucan in WS. The hydroxyl groups in glycerol can form new hydrogen-bonds with other components in DES, which might promote the dissolution performance of DES for lignin and xylan, making them more easily dissolved from WS and consequently increasing lignin and xylan removal [31]. Accordingly, glycerol was selected as the third component to synthesize the ternary DES with DES-ChCl for the subse- quent optimization of WS-pretreatment conditions.

The glycerol molar ratio in TDESGly (ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol) may have an essential for impacting the pretreatment efficiency. TDESGly (ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol) was adopted to pretreat WS (80°C, 60 min) with four molar ratios (1:1:0.5, 1:1:1, 1:1:2, and 1:1:3). As depicted in Fig. 2a, upon increasing glycerol molar ratio in ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol from 1:1:0.5 to 1:1:1, the glucan recovery elevated from 56.0% to 68.0%, and the separation ratio of lignin and xylan increased to 86.1 % and 99.9%, respectively (Fig. 2a). However, increasing the molar ratio of glycerol in this ternary DES ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol, the glucan content in WS and the separation ratio of lignin and xylan all diminished. As the molar ratio of glycerol was excessively high, the polarity of the system surpassed the optimal dissolution range for lignin and xylan, consequently diminishing their removal efficiency (Fig. 2b) [14]. The α value represents the capability of a solvent to donate protons and form hydrogen bonds with hydrogen-bond acceptors. As shown in Table 1, when the molar ratio of ChCl/p-TsOH/Gly elevated from 1:1:0.5 to 1:1:1, the α value increased significantly, indicating enhanced proton-donating capacity of the solvent, which consequently improved the pretreatment effectiveness. This was corroborated by the enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency, which increased from 92.5 % to 96.8%, as depicted in Fig. 2b. Although further increasing the molar ratio could continue to elevate the α value, Table 1 displayed that the viscosity of ChCl/p-TsOH/Gly reached its minimum at a 1:1:1 molar ratio. Viscosity is a critical physical parameter influencing pretreatment performance. Excessively high viscosity impedes efficiency in multiple ways: it hinders the penetration and diffusion of the solvent into the internal pores of the biomass, reduces effective contact with components such as lignin and hemicellulose, and decelerates the reaction rate. Consequently, as illustrated in Fig. 2b, a continued increase in the molar ratio of ChCl/p-TsOH/Gly leads to a decline in enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency. An excessive amount of glycerol may also catalyze side-reactions such as cellulose dehydration and degradation, converting cellulose into non-glucan products and consequently lowering the glucan content [32]. Accordingly, the optimal molar ratio of TDESGly (ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol) selected in this study was 1:1:1.

Pretreatment duration can considerably impact the chemical composition of WS. TDESGly ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol (molar ratio = 1:1:1, solid-liquid ratio = 1:10 wt/wt) was adopted to pretreat WS for varying durations (30 min to 75 min) at 80 °C (Fig. 3a). Upon undergoing the TDESGly-pretreatment from 30 min to 45 min, the glucan content in the TDESGly-treated WS rose from 66.2% to 70.8%, while the lignin content dropped from 17.2% to 4.8% (Fig. 3a). In 45 min, the glucan recovery reached 68.9%, and the lignin removal was as high as 88.5%, with xylan being nearly entirely eliminated. Further extension of the TDESGly-pretreatment duration didn't result in remarkable improvements in eliminating xylan and lignin. Under certain performance conditions, reactions such as lignin depolymerization and xylan hydrolysis might reach chemical equilibrium. Prolonging the operation duration no longer favored to improve the removal efficiency of these components [33]. Consequently, the optimal TDESGly-pretreatment time was determined to be 45 min.

The relationships between the combined hydrolysis factor (CHF) and residual xylan (XR), as well as between the combined delignification factor (CDF) and residual lignin (LR), can be established and fitted [37,38]. As evidenced in Fig. 5, both the CHF-XR relationship (R2 = 0.96) and the CDF-LR relationship (R2 = 0.99) exhibited strong corre- lation coefficients. As the CHF value increased from 1.7 to 10, the re- sidual xylan content decreased rapidly. A further increase in CHF from 10.0 to 35.0 resulted in a more gradual decline in residual xylan (Fig. 5a). A similar trend was observed for residual lignin content (Fig. 5b). This behavior may be attributed to the initial rapid dissolution of readily soluble free xylan, followed by the slower removal of unreacted xylan, which is tightly associated with cellulose and lignin, thereby requiring the overcoming of greater steric hindrance. Lignin removal is likely influenced by its polymeric structure-loosely bound superficial lignin is extracted first, while the internal dense cross-linked structure impedes further reaction. For the ChCl/p-TsOH/Gly pretreat- ment system, when the CHF exceeds 10.0 or the CDF exceeds 127.3, high removal rates of xylan (99.9%) and lignin (88.5%) can be achieved, indicating optimal pretreatment performance. Accordingly, XR and LR could be effectually predicted using CHF and CDF, respectively. CHF and CDF can serve as reliable indicators of TDESGly pretreatment severity. With increasing TDESGly-treatment intensity, substantial amounts of xylan and lignin were considerably eliminated [39]. Accurate prediction of lignin and xylan removal can help prevent resource waste during scale-up processes and provide robust support for the large-scale in- dustrial utilization of biomass resources in the future.

3.3. _Enzymatic digestion_ Using TDESGly ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol effectually disrupted the compact structure of biomass and separates lignin and xylan that are tightly bound to cellulose, consequently facilitating subsequent enzymolysis. Difference from untreated WS, the enzymatic digestibility of DES-pretreated WS was considerably enhanced. Under identical

treatment conditions (80 °C, 60 min), the enzymolysis efficiency of WS after TDESGly treatment reached 96.8%, which was 4.4-folds higher than that of raw WS (22.0%) (Fig. 1). In conjunction with the compositional analysis results, this improvement can be attributed to the disruption of the complex lignocellulosic matrix by TDESGly (ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol) treatment, eliminating a greater amount of lignin and exposing more cellulose surface area and enzyme-accessible sites [40,41]. Furthermore, supplementing glycerol (Gly) enables hydroxyl groups to interact with cellulose, forming a more stable structure that preserves cellulose content. This increases the substrate concentration available for enzymolysis and further improves the overall enzymolysis rate [41].

The molar ratio of the ternary DES components is a critical factor impacting enzymatic digestibility. Upon adjusting the ChCl:p-TsOH: glycerol molar ratio from 1:1:0.5 to 1:1:1 (solid-liquid ratio = 1:10 wt/ wt, 80 °C, 60 min), the enzymatic digestion rate was improved from 92.5 % to 96.8 %. Further increasing the proportion of glycerol led to a diminishment in enzymolysis efficiency (Fig. 2b). This phenomenon may be attributed to the excessive hydroxyl groups from glycerol competing with the hydrogen-bond acceptor sites originally present in the ChCl-based DES system. As a result, the system's capacity to accept protons and form hydrogen-bonds was diminished, weakening its ability to eliminate lignin and xylan. Pretreatment duration also plays a significant role in determining enzymatic digestibility. Extending the performance duration from 30 min to 45 min resulted in an increased enzymatic digestion from 87.4 % to 98.1 %. Prolonging the time to 75 min caused a decrease in hydrolysis efficiency to 94.5 % (Fig. 3b). Both insufficient and excessive operation durations are detrimental to the efficient removal of lignin and xylan, which in turn impacts the accessibility of cellulose to enzymes during the hydrolysis [40]. Operation temperature is another key parameter impacting enzymatic digestion performance (Fig. 4b). As the performance temperature was raised from 40 °C to 80 °C, the enzymatic digestion rapidly increased from 34.7 % to 98.1 %. Beyond 80 °C, the enhancement slowed. At 120 °C, the digestion rate even declined to 84.5 %. Higher performance temperatures might enhance the structural disruption of lignocellulosic materials, exposing more cellulose to enzymatic attack and thus improving hydrolysis efficiency [42]. While excessively high operation temperatures can lead to the generation of a more complex and compact structure that re-encapsulates cellulose, limiting enzyme access and consequently lowering the enzymatic digestion rate [40,43].

3.4.3. Hydrophobicity Lignin contains abundant hydrophobic groups, such as aromatic rings and aliphatic side chains. These groups can specifically interact with the hydrophobic structure of cellulase through hydrophobic forces, causing cellulase to adhere to lignin and thereby hindering the enzymatic hydrolysis process [53]. In this work, the hydrophobicity of lignin in raw WS was measured at 3.9 L/g, whereas that of WS following binary DES (ChCl:p-TsOH) treatment (80 °C, 60 min) decreased to 3.2 L/g. This is because ChCl:p-TsOH is capable of cleaving the ether bonds (e.g., the β-O-4 bond) between lignin's structural units, oxidizing the hydrophobic aromatic rings, and simultaneously reducing both the size and density of lignin's hydrophobic domains. After TDESGly (ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol) treatment, which resulted in the remarkable removal of lignin, the hydrophobicity further declined from 3.2 L/g to 2.6 L/g. Glycerol, as a hydrogen bond donor/acceptor cosolvent, promotes the cleavage of lignin by forming hydrogen bonds with the hydroxyl and carboxyl groups of lignin, while spatially inhibiting the re-aggregation of lignin fragments, thereby further reducing hydrophobicity. As evidenced in Fig. 9a, a strong negative correlation was observed between lignin hydrophobicity and both the lignin removal (R² = 0.95) and the xylan removal (R² = 0.91). The diminished lignin content led to a decrease in hydrophobic components within the DES-treated WS, consequently lowering its overall hydrophobicity. Moreover, as lignin and xylan were progressively eliminated, more cellulose becomes exposed. The hydroxyl groups present in cellulose can then interact more readily with H₂O molecules, further contributing to the reduction in lignin hydrophobicity in the pretreated WS [54]. The hydroxyl groups of cellulose establish extensive hydrogen bonding networks with water molecules, leading to the formation of a hydration layer that physically envelops the cellulose fibers and consequently repels the hydrophobic domains of lignin. Fig. 9b indicates a significant negative correlation between lignin hydrophobicity and enzymatic digestibility (R² = 0.92). As ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol treatment progressed, it cleaved the ether bonds within large lignin molecules, reduced the hydrophobic aromatic domains, and introduced additional polar functional groups, such as hydroxyl and carboxyl groups, onto the lignin fragments. These structural modifications not only decreased the number of irreversible interaction sites between lignin and cellulase but also reduced their binding affinity. Specifically, the reduction of large aromatic clusters diminished the π-π stacking interactions with the aromatic residues in cellulase, whereas the increased presence of polar groups on lignin enhanced its hydration capacity, thereby further weakened hydrophobic attractions to cellulase. Collectively, these alterations indicated a substantial decrease in lignin's hydrophobicity, which facilitated more efficient enzymatic hydrolysis [55].

The TDESGly ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly treatment strategy enhances enzy-matic digestibility by efficiently disrupting WS structure (Fig. 14). In ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly, the p-TsOH component, as a strong acidic component, may create an acidic environment in which β-O-4 bonds within lignin and glycosidic bonds in hemicellulose are readily cleaved under acidic conditions, thereby promoting lignin depolymerization and hemicellu-lose degradation [70]. Concurrently, the ChCl and Gly components in ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly can disrupt the hydrogen-bond network among cellu-lose, hemicellulose, and lignin in the WS cell wall through hydrogen-bonding interactions. This process may reduce the crystallinity of the biomass and diminish its resistance to enzymatic degradation. Incor-porating glycerol considerably increases the glucan retention rate, ul-timately enhancing enzymatic digestibility [58]. Compared with binary DES systems, TDESGly achieved higher removal efficacies for both lignin and xylan within a shorter reaction duration, revealing that supple-menting glycerol remarkably improves the pretreatment performance of DES. Glycerol can enhance lignin dissolution and acid hydrolysis of hemicellulose by modulating the acidity and hydrogen-bond network of the system [31]. Moreover, glycerol may impact the physicochemical properties of DES, such as viscosity and polarity, consequently facili-tating greater exposure of cellulose during pretreatment and further improving enzymatic digestibility [46]. A series of characterizations indicated that significant changes occurred in WS after pretreatment with ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly compared with the untreated WS. The strong acidic group of p-TsOH disrupted the compact cellulose structure. The cellulose accessibility of the treated WS reached 691.5 mg dye/g cellu-lose, while that of the untreated WS was 306.6 mg/g. Compared with untreated WS (3.9 g/L), the hydrophobicity of the treated WS decreased to 2.6 g/L. This reduction in lignin hydrophobicity partially mitigated the inhibitory effect of lignin on cellulase hydrolysis, thereby improving the enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency. Additionally, the surface area of lignin decreased after pretreatment. In a concise summary, the TDESGly-treatment system not only enhances the removal efficiency of lignin and xylan but also considerably in-creases cellulose accessibility, leading to the improved enzymolysis performance. This renders a more effective strategy for valorization of biomass resources.

Lignin itself holds considerable potential as a key precursor for manufacturing high-value materials. While the ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly treat- ment system demonstrates effective component separation, it may face challenges in fully deconstructing the macromolecular network struc- ture of lignin. Current research on the biorefining process based on TDESGly has not adequately addressed the acidic hydrolysis behavior and mechanism of WS mediated by this solvent system. On one hand, the dynamic interaction between the acidic sites within the TDESGly system and the complex structural units of WS has not been systematically investigated, which limits the ability to clearly elucidate the degradation sequence of individual components and the bond cleavage patterns during the hydrolysis process. On the other hand, there remains a lack of quantitative analysis regarding the structure-activity relationship be- tween key hydrolysis parameters and product selectivity, particularly concerning the formation of inhibitory by-products such as 5-hydroxy- methylfurfural (HMF) and furfural. ## 4. Conclusions By analyzing the alterations in chemical composition and enzymol-ysis efficiency of WS before and after three component DES treatment, TDESGly ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly (1:1:1) was screened for treating WS (80 °C, 45 min) to remove xyan, eliminate lignin, elevating subsequent enzy-matic saccharification efficiency. Afterwards, the CDF and CHF exhibi-ted significant predictive capability for delignification and xylan separation during the ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly treatment process. This predic-tive power provides a quantitative basis for optimizing DES pretreat-ment protocols. The raw materials and ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly-treated WS were characterized using FT-IR, XRD, and SEM techniques. The observed alterations in physicochemical properties and chemical composition manifested that the ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly treatment consider-ably improved cellulose accessibility, lowered lignin hydrophobicity, and diminished lignin surface area, resulting in the elevated enzymolysis efficiency. Molecular dynamics simulations showcased that strong hydrogen-bonding and van der Waals interactions existed between ChCl: p-TsOH:Gly and lignin. These findings contribute to a better under-standing of the mechanisms of ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly treatment for improving cellulase digestibility. In conclusion, this study provides a feasible and sustainable solution for biomass processing based on TDES ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly technology, enabling effectual treatment under rela-tively mild operational conditions and realizing the valorization of lignocellulosic biomass into high-value products.

The combined hydrolysis factor and combined delignification factor quantitatively predicted the dissolution kinetics of residual xylan and residual lignin, respectively, with high accuracy. Following ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly treatment, the accessibility of cellulose in wheat straw elevated considerably to 691.5 mg dye/g cellulose, while surface lignin area diminished to 134.6 m²/g and lignin hydrophobicity was weakened to 2.6 L/g. These structural and surface property modifications contributed to the enhancement of enzymolysis. Molecular dynamics simulations and quantum chemical calculations were adopted to reveal van der Waals interactions between ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly and lignin, as well as dispersion interactions between ChCl and lignin, consequently elucidating the molecular-level interaction mechanism between lignocellulose and ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly. In summary, this study achieved effectual pretreatment of wheat straw using the TDES ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly but also considerably promoted the depolymerization of lignocellulosic biomass in biorefining processes, offering new insights into the value-added utilization of biomass resources. 1. Introduction To date, the development of clean energy alternatives has emerged as a critical priority [1,2]. Lignocellulosic biomass exhibits considerable potential for manufacturing bio-based materials, bioethanol, and bio-diesel [3,4]. Wheat straw (WS), a widely available byproduct of global wheat cultivation, is often treated as waste, yet it contains a significant amount of polysaccharides, primarily composed of approximately 70 % sugar compounds, including cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin [5,6]. Nevertheless, the complex structural interactions between cellulose and hemicellulose hinder enzymatic digestion [7,8]. Accordingly, it is essential to develop and select appropriate pretreatment strategies to overcome the recalcitrance of lignocellulosic materials and facilitate their effective disintegration [9]. Recently, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged as promising green solvents to pretreat biomass due to their tailorable hydrogen- * Corresponding author. E-mail addresses: heyucai2001@163.com, yucaihe@cczu.edu.cn (Y.-C. He). 1 They contributed equally to this work. bonding networks, low toxicity, and excellent recyclability [10–12]. For instance, Li et al. reported an acidic binary DES composed of ChCl/ oxalic acid (molar ratio 3:1) that achieved 84% delignification and 96% enzymolysis efficiency after optimized treatment (130 °C, 1 h) of rape- seed straw [13]. Similarly, Tang et al. demonstrated that pretreatment with an acidic binary DES system of cetyltrimethylammonium bromide/ glycerol (molar ratio 1:6, 200 °C, 90 min) resulted in 46 % delignifica- tion and 53% xylan removal from rapeseed straw [14]. Recent studies indicated that incorporating a third component (such as alcoholic compounds, Lewis acids) into binary DESs to form ternary DESs (TDESs) can considerably improve biomass pretreatment efficiency [15–17]. Introducing a third component markedly modulates the physicochem- ical features of the solvent system (such as viscosity and dissolving ca- pacity), consequently improving mass transfer rates and overall pretreatment efficiency [18,19]. The determination of K-T parameters of TDESs The Kamlet-Taft parameters are empirical descriptors adopted to characterize the microscopic properties of solvent molecules and to quantitatively assess the specific interactions between solvents and solutes [26]. In this study, we systematically investigated the effects of EG) and Gly as hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) on the solvation properties of DES-ChCl. Specifically, EG and Gly were introduced into the DES-ChCl system at identical molar ratios, and the Kamlet-Taft parameters of the resulting binary DESs (designated as TDES$_{EG}$ and TDES$_{Gly}$, respectively) were accurately measured (Table 1). The experimental results clearly demonstrated that, compared with TDES$_{EG}$, TDES$_{Gly}$ exhibited significantly higher hydrogen bond donor ability (α value), hydrogen bond acceptor ability (β value), and dipolarity/polarizability (π* value). This notable difference in solvation properties is primarily attributed to the fundamental structural differences between Gly and EG—specifically, Gly contains an additional hydroxyl (-OH) functional group compared to EG. This additional hydroxyl group exerts a dual influence: first, it enhances the acidity of glycerol, providing more hydrogen bond donor sites and thereby directly increasing its hydrogen bond donor ability (α value); second, due to the high electronegativity of the oxygen atom, this hydroxyl group also significantly enhances Gly's capacity as a hydrogen bond acceptor (β value) [27]. Moreover, the molecular structure of glycerol is more complex, and its electron cloud distribution is more responsive to external electric fields, leading to greater polarizability, which is reflected in the significantly elevated π* value [27]. Given the overall advantages of TDES$_{Gly}$ in terms of α, β, and π* parameters—factors directly associated with the dissolution capacity, catalytic activity, and interaction strength with substrates (e.g., biomass) of DESs—Gly was selected as the optimal third component for constructing a novel TDES system in combination with ChCl and p-TsOH, based on its superior solvation characteristics. The molar ratio of DES is a critical factor influencing the Kamlet-Taft parameters. In this work, TDESGly was prepared with varying molar ratios (1:1:0.5, 1:1:1, 1:1:2, 1:1:3), and the impacts of these ratios on the Kamlet-Taft parameter values were systematically estimated. As the molar ratio of glycerol (Gly) elevated, the α and π* values of the Kamlet-Taft parameters gradually increased, whereas the β value showed a corresponding decrease (Table 1). Hydrophobicity Lignin contains abundant hydrophobic groups, such as aromatic rings and aliphatic side chains. These groups can specifically interact with the hydrophobic structure of cellulase through hydrophobic forces, causing cellulase to adhere to lignin and thereby hindering the enzymatic hydrolysis process [53]. In this work, the hydrophobicity of lignin in raw WS was measured at 3.9 L/g, whereas that of WS following binary DES (ChCl:p-TsOH) treatment (80 °C, 60 min) decreased to 3.2 L/g. This is because ChCl:p-TsOH is capable of cleaving the ether bonds (e.g., the β-O-4 bond) between lignin's structural units, oxidizing the hydrophobic aromatic rings, and simultaneously reducing both the size and density of lignin's hydrophobic domains. After TDESGly (ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol) treatment, which resulted in the remarkable removal of lignin, the hydrophobicity further declined from 3.2 L/g to 2.6 L/g. Glycerol, as a hydrogen bond donor/acceptor cosolvent, promotes the cleavage of lignin by forming hydrogen bonds with the hydroxyl and carboxyl groups of lignin, while spatially inhibiting the re-aggregation of lignin fragments, thereby further reducing hydrophobicity. As evidenced in Fig. 9a, a strong negative correlation was observed between lignin hydrophobicity and both the lignin removal (R² = 0.95) and the xylan removal (R² = 0.91). The diminished lignin content led to a decrease in hydrophobic components within the DES-treated WS, consequently lowering its overall hydrophobicity. Moreover, as lignin and xylan were progressively eliminated, more cellulose becomes exposed. The hydroxyl groups present in cellulose can then interact more readily with H₂O molecules, further contributing to the reduction in lignin hydrophobicity in the pretreated WS [54]. The hydroxyl groups of cellulose establish extensive hydrogen bonding networks with water molecules, leading to the formation of a hydration layer that physically envelops the cellulose fibers and consequently repels the hydrophobic domains of lignin. Fig. 9b indicates a significant negative correlation between lignin hydrophobicity and enzymatic digestibility (R² = 0.92). As ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol treatment progressed, it cleaved the ether bonds within large lignin molecules, reduced the hydrophobic aromatic domains, and introduced additional polar functional groups, such as hydroxyl and carboxyl groups, onto the lignin fragments. These structural modifications not only decreased the number of irreversible interaction sites between lignin and cellulase but also reduced their binding affinity. Specifically, the reduction of large aromatic clusters diminished the π-π stacking interactions with the aromatic residues in cellulase, whereas the increased presence of polar groups on lignin enhanced its hydration capacity, thereby further weakened hydrophobic attractions to cellulase. Collectively, these alterations indicated a substantial decrease in lignin's hydrophobicity, which facilitated more efficient enzymatic hydrolysis [55]. 3.5. The raw materials and ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly-treated WS were characterized using FT-IR, XRD, and SEM techniques. The observed alterations in physicochemical properties and chemical composition manifested that the ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly treatment consider-ably improved cellulose accessibility, lowered lignin hydrophobicity, and diminished lignin surface area, resulting in the elevated enzymolysis efficiency. Molecular dynamics simulations showcased that strong hydrogen-bonding and van der Waals interactions existed between ChCl: p-TsOH:Gly and lignin. These findings contribute to a better under-standing of the mechanisms of ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly treatment for improving cellulase digestibility. In conclusion, this study provides a feasible and sustainable solution for biomass processing based on TDES ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly technology, enabling effectual treatment under rela-tively mild operational conditions and realizing the valorization of lignocellulosic biomass into high-value products. The combined hydrolysis factor and combined delignification factor quantitatively predicted the dissolution kinetics of residual xylan and residual lignin, respectively, with high accuracy. Following ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly treatment, the accessibility of cellulose in wheat straw elevated considerably to 691.5 mg dye/g cellulose, while surface lignin area diminished to 134.6 m²/g and lignin hydrophobicity was weakened to 2.6 L/g. These structural and surface property modifications contributed to the enhancement of enzymolysis. Molecular dynamics simulations and quantum chemical calculations were adopted to reveal van der Waals interactions between ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly and lignin, as well as dispersion interactions between ChCl and lignin, consequently elucidating the molecular-level interaction mechanism between lignocellulose and ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly. In summary, this study achieved effectual pretreatment of wheat straw using the TDES ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly but also considerably promoted the depolymerization of lignocellulosic biomass in biorefining processes, offering new insights into the value-added utilization of biomass resources. 1. Introduction To date, the development of clean energy alternatives has emerged as a critical priority [1,2]. Lignocellulosic biomass exhibits considerable potential for manufacturing bio-based materials, bioethanol, and bio-diesel [3,4]. Wheat straw (WS), a widely available byproduct of global wheat cultivation, is often treated as waste, yet it contains a significant amount of polysaccharides, primarily composed of approximately 70 % sugar compounds, including cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin [5,6]. Nevertheless, the complex structural interactions between cellulose and hemicellulose hinder enzymatic digestion [7,8]. Accordingly, it is essential to develop and select appropriate pretreatment strategies to overcome the recalcitrance of lignocellulosic materials and facilitate their effective disintegration [9]. Recently, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged as promising green solvents to pretreat biomass due to their tailorable hydrogen- * Corresponding author. E-mail addresses: heyucai2001@163.com, yucaihe@cczu.edu.cn (Y.-C. He). 1 They contributed equally to this work. bonding networks, low toxicity, and excellent recyclability [10–12]. For instance, Li et al. reported an acidic binary DES composed of ChCl/ oxalic acid (molar ratio 3:1) that achieved 84% delignification and 96% enzymolysis efficiency after optimized treatment (130 °C, 1 h) of rape- seed straw [13]. Similarly, Tang et al. demonstrated that pretreatment with an acidic binary DES system of cetyltrimethylammonium bromide/ glycerol (molar ratio 1:6, 200 °C, 90 min) resulted in 46 % delignifica- tion and 53% xylan removal from rapeseed straw [14]. Recent studies indicated that incorporating a third component (such as alcoholic compounds, Lewis acids) into binary DESs to form ternary DESs (TDESs) can considerably improve biomass pretreatment efficiency [15–17]. Introducing a third component markedly modulates the physicochem- ical features of the solvent system (such as viscosity and dissolving ca- pacity), consequently improving mass transfer rates and overall pretreatment efficiency [18,19]. Functional groups like hydroxyls introduced by the third component can strengthen the hydrogen- https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijbiomac.2025.147895 Received 10 August 2025; Received in revised form 11 September 2025; Accepted 23 September 2025 Available online 24 September 2025 0141-8130/© 2025 Elsevier B.V. International Journal of Biological Macromolecules 330 (2025) 147895 bonding network, which not only facilitates lower melting points enabling milder pretreatment temperatures but also augments the effectual separation of biomass components [20–22]. Compared to conventional thermochemical methods which typically require reaction temperatures exceeding 200 °C to achieve effective biomass decompo- sition, TDES based approaches enable efficient biomass conversion under significantly milder conditions (e.g., 80–120 °C). This substantial reduction in operating temperature not only directly diminishes energy input requirements but also mitigates additional costs associated with high-temperature-resistant equipment, thereby achieving considerable energy savings. Furthermore, the mild reaction conditions minimize excessive degradation of high-value components within the biomass, enhancing selectivity toward target products. Collectively, these ad- vantages position TDES-mediated processes as a more sustainable technological pathway for biomass valorization. For example, Zhao et al. fabricated a TDES using octadecyl dimethyl ammonium chloride, pro- pionic acid, and p-toluenesulfonic acid (p-TsOH), achieving effectual pretreatment of sorghum straw under relatively mild conditions with an enzymolysis efficiency of 69.3% [23]. Zhang et al. prepared a TDES from choline chloride (ChCl), N-(2-hydroxyethyl)ethylenediamine (NE), and iron(III) chloride for corn stover treatment under mild conditions, achieving 87% delignification [24]. Similarly, He et al. reported that a TDES composed of ChCl, glycerol (Gly), and aluminum chloride removed 70.8% lignin and 87.7% hemicellulose from reed straw [25]. Consequently, TDES technology enables the effectual conversion of previously underutilized biomass resources, apparently broadening the scope of biorefinery feedstocks and opening new pathways toward enhancing the economic viability and sustainability of full biomass component utilization. This work aimed to develop an effectual pretreatment process for wheat straw (WS) based on a DES system composed of choline chloride (ChCl), p-toluenesulfonic acid (p-TsOH), and glycerol (Gly), with the objective of enhancing its physicochemical properties and microstructural characteristics. The two-phase combined hydrolysis factor (CHF) model and the combined delignification factor (CDF) model can be utilized to quantitatively characterize the processes of hemicellulose dissolution and lignin removal, respectively. The effectiveness of the pretreatment can be estimated by analyzing variations in component content and enzymolysis performance, while key operational parameters—such as performance temperature, operation duration, and molar ratio—are systematically optimized. The response surface methodology can be adopted to determine the optimal DES-treatment conditions and to estimate the enzymatic digestion rate as a response variable. Systematically investigating the regulatory of the pretreatment on influencing cellulose accessibility, surface lignin coverage, and hydrophobicity can be implemented to assess the impacts on the subsequent enzymolysis efficiency. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and other analytical techniques may be utilized to characterize the structural and compositional alterations in WS before and after DES treatment, consequently elucidating the mechanisms underlying lignin removal and enhanced enzymolysis. To explore the interaction mechanisms between biomass and DES at the molecular level, molecular dynamics simulations can be adopted, offering theoretical insights for the development of efficient biomass pretreatment strategies. Overall, this study presents a comprehensive analysis and in-depth discussion of the ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly-based biomass pretreatment process. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Preparation of DESs ChCl, _p_-TsOH, and glycerol were blended at varying molar ratios (1:1:0.5, 1:1:1, 1:1:2, 1:1:3). Concurrently, ChCl and _p_-TsOH were individually combined with ethylene glycol (EG) at a molar ratio of 1:1:1. The DES preparation was implemented at 80 °C for 15 to 30 min, and the obtained homogeneous and transparent liquids were used to pretreat WS without further purification. ## 2.2. Treatment of WS with DESS In a three-necked flask, 60 g of TDES and 6 g of WS were mixed, resulting in a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:10 (w/w). The mixture was stirred uniformly in an oil bath at a pre-determined temperature range of 40–120 °C for a variable duration of 30–75 min. ## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. The determination of K-T parameters of TDESs The Kamlet-Taft parameters are empirical descriptors adopted to characterize the microscopic properties of solvent molecules and to quantitatively assess the specific interactions between solvents and solutes [26]. In this study, we systematically investigated the effects of EG) and Gly as hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) on the solvation properties of DES-ChCl. Specifically, EG and Gly were introduced into the DES-ChCl system at identical molar ratios, and the Kamlet-Taft parameters of the resulting binary DESs (designated as TDES$_{EG}$ and TDES$_{Gly}$, respectively) were accurately measured (Table 1). Hydrophobicity Lignin contains abundant hydrophobic groups, such as aromatic rings and aliphatic side chains. These groups can specifically interact with the hydrophobic structure of cellulase through hydrophobic forces, causing cellulase to adhere to lignin and thereby hindering the enzymatic hydrolysis process [53]. In this work, the hydrophobicity of lignin in raw WS was measured at 3.9 L/g, whereas that of WS following binary DES (ChCl:p-TsOH) treatment (80 °C, 60 min) decreased to 3.2 L/g. This is because ChCl:p-TsOH is capable of cleaving the ether bonds (e.g., the β-O-4 bond) between lignin's structural units, oxidizing the hydrophobic aromatic rings, and simultaneously reducing both the size and density of lignin's hydrophobic domains. After TDESGly (ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol) treatment, which resulted in the remarkable removal of lignin, the hydrophobicity further declined from 3.2 L/g to 2.6 L/g. Glycerol, as a hydrogen bond donor/acceptor cosolvent, promotes the cleavage of lignin by forming hydrogen bonds with the hydroxyl and carboxyl groups of lignin, while spatially inhibiting the re-aggregation of lignin fragments, thereby further reducing hydrophobicity. As evidenced in Fig. 9a, a strong negative correlation was observed between lignin hydrophobicity and both the lignin removal (R² = 0.95) and the xylan removal (R² = 0.91). The diminished lignin content led to a decrease in hydrophobic components within the DES-treated WS, consequently lowering its overall hydrophobicity. Moreover, as lignin and xylan were progressively eliminated, more cellulose becomes exposed. The hydroxyl groups present in cellulose can then interact more readily with H₂O molecules, further contributing to the reduction in lignin hydrophobicity in the pretreated WS [54]. The hydroxyl groups of cellulose establish extensive hydrogen bonding networks with water molecules, leading to the formation of a hydration layer that physically envelops the cellulose fibers and consequently repels the hydrophobic domains of lignin. Fig. 9b indicates a significant negative correlation between lignin hydrophobicity and enzymatic digestibility (R² = 0.92). As ChCl:p-TsOH:glycerol treatment progressed, it cleaved the ether bonds within large lignin molecules, reduced the hydrophobic aromatic domains, and introduced additional polar functional groups, such as hydroxyl and carboxyl groups, onto the lignin fragments. These structural modifications not only decreased the number of irreversible interaction sites between lignin and cellulase but also reduced their binding affinity. Specifically, the reduction of large aromatic clusters diminished the π-π stacking interactions with the aromatic residues in cellulase, whereas the increased presence of polar groups on lignin enhanced its hydration capacity, thereby further weakened hydrophobic attractions to cellulase. Collectively, these alterations indicated a substantial decrease in lignin's hydrophobicity, which facilitated more efficient enzymatic hydrolysis [55]. 3.5. Conclusions By analyzing the alterations in chemical composition and enzymol-ysis efficiency of WS before and after three component DES treatment, TDESGly ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly (1:1:1) was screened for treating WS (80 °C, 45 min) to remove xyan, eliminate lignin, elevating subsequent enzy-matic saccharification efficiency. This predic-tive power provides a quantitative basis for optimizing DES pretreat-ment protocols. The raw materials and ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly-treated WS were characterized using FT-IR, XRD, and SEM techniques. The observed alterations in physicochemical properties and chemical composition manifested that the ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly treatment consider-ably improved cellulose accessibility, lowered lignin hydrophobicity, and diminished lignin surface area, resulting in the elevated enzymolysis efficiency. Molecular dynamics simulations showcased that strong hydrogen-bonding and van der Waals interactions existed between ChCl: p-TsOH:Gly and lignin. These findings contribute to a better under-standing of the mechanisms of ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly treatment for improving cellulase digestibility. In conclusion, this study provides a feasible and sustainable solution for biomass processing based on TDES ChCl:p-TsOH:Gly technology, enabling effectual treatment under rela-tively mild operational conditions and realizing the valorization of lignocellulosic biomass into high-value products.
